summary: Gives guidance, based on operational experience, on choosing NSEC3 parameters for DNSSEC. NSEC3 proves that a name does not exist without exposing neighboring names directly. This Best Current Practice updates RFC 5155 with advice about selecting parameters.

eli5.summary: DNSSEC must prove a name does not exist without handing out a list of real names. Scrambling names makes this possible, and this document says how much scrambling is worth it.

should i use a salt with nsec3
subtitle: Keep NSEC3 simple: zero extra iterations, no salt, and resolvers that refuse costly settings.

tldr.problem: NSEC3 has tunable parameters (iterations and salt) but there was no published guidance on good values, and high settings cost CPU while adding little protection.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends NSEC3PARAM settings of SHA-1, 0 extra iterations and an empty salt, and tells validating resolvers they may treat higher iteration counts as insecure or answer SERVFAIL.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 5155 and sets a single recommended configuration for all zones, plus a new Extended DNS Error code 27 for unsupported iteration counts.

today: RFC 9276 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 236) that updates RFC 5155, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. It significantly decreases the requirements originally given in Section 10.3 of RFC 5155.

sections.title: What NSEC3 Is and Why Parameters Matter
sections.content:
NSEC3 gives DNSSEC a way to prove that a name does not exist, using signed records. Unlike NSEC, it hides the real names in a zone by hashing them. The RFC notes that only SHA-1 is in use on the Internet.

NSEC3 also offers opt-out, where one NSEC3 record can cover a block of unsigned delegations. That saves memory and CPU but weakens the tamper resistance of the proof.

The settings live in an NSEC3PARAM record at the zone apex: the hash algorithm, the flags, the number of hash iterations and the salt. This document gives best-practice advice for them and updates RFC 5155.
sections.eli5: NSEC3 is a way to say "that name is not here" without showing everyone the list of names that are. It has a few dials, and this document says where to set them.

sections.title: Algorithm, Flags and Opt-Out
sections.content:
The algorithm field is not discussed; the RFC points readers to RFC 8624 for DNSSEC algorithm guidance. The flags field in NSEC3PARAM currently holds only reserved and unassigned flags, but each NSEC3 record carries an Opt-Out flag.

Opt-out should only be used in large, highly dynamic zones with a small percentage of signed delegations, such as registration points whose updates outpace real-time signing or that run on memory-constrained hardware. Smaller zones, or large but relatively static ones, are encouraged not to use it. Operators are also told to weigh the costs and benefits of choosing NSEC3 over NSEC at all.
sections.eli5: There is a shortcut switch that skips some paperwork. It is only worth using for a gigantic, fast-changing list. Everyone else should leave it off.

sections.title: Iterations and Salt
sections.content:
The first hash is typically enough to discourage zone walking. RFC 5155 defines the Iterations field as the number of additional times the hash is performed, so a value of 0 still means one hash.

Extra iterations buy little. Most names are meant to be memorable and appear in many logs, and a simple dictionary of prefixes such as www, mail and imap reveals many labels. A determined attacker with resources will find most guessable names regardless, so extra iterations mean rising cost with diminishing returns.

The salt is also of little use. Hashed names are already implicitly salted by the zone's FQDN, so no single precomputed table works against several zones. An extra salt only raises attack cost if it changes during the online phase of a zone-walking attack. Changing it needs a whole new NSEC3 chain, so frequent re-salting is impractical, which makes the salt field functionally useless.
sections.eli5: Mixing a secret more and more times does not stop a patient thief who can guess common words. A fixed extra ingredient does not help either, because it is the same every time.

sections.title: Advice for Zone Publishers
sections.content:
If NSEC3's operational or security features are not needed, publishers SHOULD use NSEC instead, because NSEC3 costs more computation for authoritative servers and validating clients. If NSEC3 must be used, an iterations count of 0 MUST be used. Other counts increase the impact of CPU-exhausting DoS attacks and the risk of interoperability problems.

The recommended parameters for all zones are shown as bcp.example. IN NSEC3PARAM 1 0 0 -: SHA-1, no extra iterations, empty salt. Operators SHOULD NOT use a salt. Opt-out is NOT RECOMMENDED for small zones and MAY be used for very large, sparsely signed zones where most records are insecure delegations.

If a salt is used anyway, the iterations and salt can be changed without waiting for caches to expire, because validating resolvers do not use NSEC3PARAM. A complete new NSEC3 chain must be built and the full zone re-signed.
sections.eli5: If you do not need the fancy hiding, use the simple method. If you do, use the plainest settings: no extra rounds and no extra ingredient.

sections.title: Advice for Validating Resolvers and Secondaries
sections.content:
Open validating resolvers face compute limits when serving anonymous clients, so resolver operators and implementers are encouraged to lower their acceptable iteration limits over time and to lower their default limit for returning SERVFAIL. A validating resolver MAY return an insecure response, or MAY return SERVFAIL, when NSEC3 iterations are larger than 0. An insecure response MUST still come after validating the signature over the NSEC3 record.

Resolvers that return an insecure or SERVFAIL answer after validating an unsupported parameter SHOULD attach an Extended DNS Error with value 27. Resolvers that simply ignore such a response without validating the signature MUST NOT return it.

When primary and secondary servers are run by different staff or software, operators of secondaries should advertise the limits they support, and primaries should check that their secondaries support the planned parameters. After changing iteration counts, a primary should query its secondaries with known nonexistent labels to verify they respond as expected.
sections.eli5: A busy helper is allowed to say "this is too much work, I will not check it." If it does, it should say why. Teammates should also check that they can all handle the same rules.

sections.title: Security, Operations and Measurements
sections.content:
The whole document is about security and operational tradeoffs. One point is called out: if a resolver treats a zone as insecure above one iteration value (the RFC's example is 100) and returns SERVFAIL above a higher one (500), the zone is exposed to attacker-in-the-middle attacks as if it were unsigned between them. Operators and implementers SHOULD set the two thresholds to the same value.

Appendix A reports that at publication time an upper limit of 100 iterations for treating a zone as insecure was interoperable without significant problems, but still allowed CPU-exhausting DoS attacks, and that returning SERVFAIL beyond 500 iterations also appeared interoperable.

Appendix B shows the cost: authoritative query throughput falls as iterations rise, for example to 89% of the zero-iteration rate at 10 iterations, 47% at 100 and 38% at 150.
sections.eli5: If one rule says "suspicious" at 100 and another says "stop" at 500, a trickster can sneak through in between. Using the same line for both closes the gap.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA allocated Extended DNS Error code 27, "Unsupported NSEC3 iterations value", in the First Come First Served range of the "Extended DNS Error Codes" registry. The reference is RFC 9276.
sections.eli5: A new numbered label, 27, was added to a public list so resolvers can all explain this particular problem the same way.
